passage: I'm Avni, and I've worked beside Wasim at the hospital lab for a year. Our shifts rotate every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights. Lately Wasim eats biscuits from the drawer instead of meals, yawns through handovers, and last Tuesday he slammed a tray down when a ward boy asked about a delayed report. That's not the Wasim I know. At tea I asked if he was all right. He rubbed his eyes and said he couldn't remember the last time he'd slept properly. I told him about the free check-up at the staff clinic, and that our supervisor once let me stay on one shift pattern for a month when I asked. He did both. I don't know how he feels inside, but he's packing lunch again.

qa.q: How often do the lab shifts rotate?
qa.a: Every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights.

qa.q: What does Wasim slamming the tray suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed exhausted and short-tempered; broken sleep from the rotating shifts had worn his patience thin.
A check-up at the staff clinic and asking the supervisor for a steadier shift pattern protect Wasim's health, since predictable hours help sleep, meals and mood.

qa.q: How might the ward boy have felt when Wasim slammed the tray?
qa.a: He was probably startled and a bit hurt, since he had only asked about a delayed report.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, a worker whose rotating shifts disrupt sleep, meals and mood, and who is steered towards a steadier pattern and a health check-up.

passage: March: Nilesh's shifts at the textile mill flipped every few days. He ate dinner at breakfast time, dozed on the bus, and barked at his roommate Darshan for rattling a steel glass. Headaches came most afternoons, and he brushed them off with more tea. April, one Sunday: Nilesh sat down with his supervisor and asked for a steadier rotation. The supervisor agreed to longer blocks on the same shift. That week Darshan went with him to the clinic by the mill gate for a check-up; the doctor asked about sleep and meals and told him to come back if the headaches kept going or worried him. May: Nilesh cooked dal on his day off, slept at the same time most nights, and apologised to Darshan about the glass.

qa.q: What did the supervisor agree to?
qa.a: Longer blocks on the same shift.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling in March, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was exhausted and irritable; he dozed on the bus, barked at Darshan over a rattling glass and had headaches most afternoons.

qa.q: Which choices were the turning point for Nilesh?
qa.a: Asking the supervisor for a steadier rotation and getting a check-up at the clinic, which made his sleep and meals more predictable and put his health in a doctor's view.

qa.q: What was it like for Darshan to share a room with Nilesh in March?
qa.a: Darshan was likely on edge, getting snapped at over small noises, yet still cared enough to go to the clinic with Nilesh.

grounding: Shows a worker whose changing shifts disrupt sleep, meals and mood, and how a more predictable pattern and a health check-up protect long-term wellbeing.
